name: Vectors
summary: An ordered list of numbers that represents a point or a direction in space.
key_points: a vector is an ordered list of numbers
it has a length (magnitude) and a direction
vectors are added and scaled component by component

probe.q: In one or two sentences: what is a vector, and what does it mean to add two vectors?

name: Dot product
summary: The sum of element-wise products of two equal-length vectors; it measures how aligned they are.
key_points: multiply matching components then sum them
the result is a single number (a scalar)
large and positive when vectors point the same way, zero when perpendicular

probe.q: Compute the dot product of [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6], and say what it measures.

name: Matrix multiplication
summary: Each output entry is the dot product of a row of A with a column of B; the inner dimensions must match.
key_points: each output entry is a dot product of a row and a column
the inner dimensions must match
an (m x n) times (n x p) matrix gives an (m x p) matrix

probe.q: If A is 2x3 and B is 3x4, what is the shape of A·B and how is each entry computed?

name: Cosine similarity
summary: The dot product divided by the product of the two vector lengths; it compares direction and ignores magnitude.
key_points: dot product divided by the product of the two lengths
it compares direction and ignores magnitude
1 means same direction, 0 means unrelated, -1 means opposite

probe.q: What does a cosine similarity of 1, of 0, and of -1 tell you about two vectors?

name: Derivatives
summary: The instantaneous rate of change of a function: the slope of its tangent line at a point.
key_points: a derivative is the instantaneous rate of change
it is the slope of the tangent line at a point
it says how much the output moves for a tiny change in the input

probe.q: What does the derivative of a function at a point tell you?

name: Partial derivatives
summary: The derivative with respect to one variable while every other variable is held constant.
key_points: differentiate with respect to one variable only
all other variables are treated as constants
each partial derivative measures sensitivity to one input

probe.q: For f(x, y) = x^2 * y, what is the partial derivative with respect to x, and what do you do with y?

name: Chain rule
summary: The derivative of a composition f(g(x)) is f'(g(x)) multiplied by g'(x).
key_points: the derivative of f(g(x)) is f'(g(x)) times g'(x)
derivatives of nested functions multiply, they do not add
differentiate the outer function then multiply by the inner derivative

probe.q: What is d/dx of f(g(x))? Give the rule in words or symbols.

name: Gradients
summary: The vector of all partial derivatives; it points in the direction of steepest increase.
key_points: the gradient is the vector of all partial derivatives
it points in the direction of steepest increase
moving against it decreases the function fastest

probe.q: Which direction does the gradient of a loss point, and how would you use it to reduce the loss?

name: Gradient descent
summary: Repeatedly update parameters by stepping against the gradient: w = w - lr * grad.
key_points: update parameters with w = w - learning_rate * gradient
step against the gradient to go downhill on the loss
a learning rate that is too large overshoots and can diverge

probe.q: Write the gradient descent update rule and say what happens if the learning rate is too large.

name: Computational graphs
summary: A directed graph whose nodes are operations and whose edges carry values, so gradients can flow backwards node by node.
key_points: nodes are operations and edges carry values
the forward pass computes outputs node by node
gradients flow backwards using each node's local derivative

probe.q: What is a computational graph and why does it make computing gradients easy?

name: Backpropagation
summary: Efficiently applies the chain rule backwards through a computational graph to get the gradient for every parameter.
key_points: the forward pass computes predictions and the loss
the backward pass applies the chain rule from the loss back to each parameter
it reuses intermediate results so all gradients cost about one extra pass

probe.q: Explain backpropagation in two sentences: what happens in the forward pass and what happens in the backward pass?

name: Probability basics
summary: Probabilities are non-negative numbers between 0 and 1 that sum to 1 across mutually exclusive outcomes.
key_points: every probability is between 0 and 1
probabilities of all outcomes sum to 1
a distribution assigns a probability to each possible outcome

probe.q: What two properties must a probability distribution over classes satisfy?

name: Softmax
summary: Turns a vector of scores into a probability distribution: exp(x_i) / sum_j exp(x_j).
key_points: softmax exponentiates each score then divides by the sum
the outputs are positive and sum to 1
subtracting the max score first avoids overflow without changing the result

probe.q: What does softmax output, and why is subtracting the max score before exponentiating a common trick?

name: Cross-entropy loss
summary: Loss = -log(probability assigned to the true class); it punishes confident wrong predictions heavily.
key_points: the loss is the negative log of the probability given to the true class
it is small when the model is confident and right
it grows very large when the model is confident and wrong

probe.q: A model gives the true class probability 0.9 in one case and 0.1 in another. Which has lower cross-entropy loss, and why?

name: Linear layer
summary: Computes y = W x + b: a learned matrix multiply followed by a bias shift.
key_points: it computes y = Wx + b
W (weights) and b (bias) are the learned parameters
each output is a weighted sum of all inputs

probe.q: What does a linear layer compute, and which parts are learned?

name: Activation functions
summary: Non-linear functions (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh) applied after linear layers; without them stacked layers collapse into one linear map.
key_points: activations add non-linearity between layers
without them any stack of linear layers equals a single linear layer
ReLU, sigmoid and tanh are common choices

probe.q: Why do neural networks need non-linear activation functions between linear layers?

name: Embeddings
summary: Learned dense vectors that place similar tokens or items close together in space.
key_points: an embedding is a learned dense vector for a token or item
similar meanings end up close together
closeness is measured with distance or cosine similarity

probe.q: What is an embedding and what does it mean for two embeddings to be close?

name: Attention
summary: Each token scores every other token with scaled dot products (Q·Kᵀ/√d), softmaxes the scores, and takes a weighted sum of the values.
key_points: queries are compared with keys using dot products
scores are scaled by sqrt(d) then passed through softmax
the softmax weights are used to average the values

probe.q: In scaled dot-product attention, what are Q, K and V, and why divide the scores by sqrt(d)?

name: Positional encoding
summary: Adds position information to token embeddings because attention on its own ignores word order.
key_points: attention alone has no notion of token order
position vectors are added to the token embeddings
this lets the model tell 'dog bites man' from 'man bites dog'

probe.q: Why do transformers need positional encodings?

name: Transformers
summary: Stacks of self-attention and feed-forward blocks with residual connections and normalisation, running on embeddings plus positions.
key_points: each block has self-attention followed by a feed-forward network
residual connections and layer normalisation stabilise deep stacks
input is token embeddings plus positional encodings

probe.q: Name the main building blocks of a transformer block.
